items.prompt: What does 'bus factor' count?
choices: Tasks one person finishes per week
Meetings held about shared risks
People whose absence would stall critical work
items.explanation: It counts how many people can become unavailable before the work has nobody left who can do it.

items.prompt: A job has a bus factor of one. What does that mean?
choices: The job needs exactly one person at a time
One departure would leave nobody able to do it
Only a single person is allowed to ask questions about it
items.explanation: A bus factor of one means a single absence is enough to stall the job.

items.prompt: Which situation is a bus factor problem?
choices: Two people disagree about naming conventions
A job runs slowly every night after midnight
Only one person can approve payment deploys
items.explanation: The risk is about who can do the work, not about style or speed.

items.prompt: Is bus factor only about people quitting?
choices: Yes: it only matters when someone resigns
Yes: it only matters when someone is dismissed
No: illness, leave or any absence exposes it
items.explanation: Any absence reveals the same concentration, whatever causes it.

items.prompt: What is 'knowledge concentration'?
choices: Understanding of a system living mostly in one head
A team agreeing on one shared way of working
All of the documentation being kept inside one long file
items.explanation: Concentration means the knowledge is held by very few people, often one.

items.prompt: What does 'knowledge distribution' mean?
choices: Giving each teammate a separate system to own entirely alone
Spreading understanding of key systems across several people
Sending every single teammate the same weekly status update
items.explanation: Distribution is the deliberate opposite of concentration.

items.prompt: What is 'succession'?
choices: Promoting the longest-serving person each year
Hiring a replacement only after somebody has resigned
Having someone who could plausibly step into a role
items.explanation: Succession is about having a credible second person before they are needed.

items.prompt: Is a bus factor of three better than one?
choices: No: more people knowing means more confusion
Yes: the team can absorb a departure
No: fewer people knowing is always safer
items.explanation: More people able to do the job means one absence is survivable.

items.prompt: Scores for the billing job: Priya 3, Dan 0, Wren 1, Sam 0 (3 means fully independent, 1 means has only seen it). What is its bus factor?
choices: Two: Priya and Wren both have real exposure to the job already
Four: everyone on the team could in principle be trained for it
One: only Priya can run it alone, and Wren has only seen it
Zero: nobody besides Priya was ever formally assigned to the job
items.explanation: Only people who can run the job independently count. Wren has seen it, which is a 1, not the ability to run it alone.
items.reference:
Billing job: who can run it alone?
🧑‍💻 Priya: 3 (fully independent)
Dan: 0   Wren: 1   Sam: 0
One person can run it alone: bus factor 1
Why: bus factor counts how many people can vanish before nobody is left who can do a specific job.
items.learnMore:
Bus factor is per responsibility

A team has no single bus factor. Each critical job has its own, set by how many people can really run it alone. The number is found by looking at the work, not at the headcount.

Common mistake

Counting everyone who has ever seen a job as someone who could run it.
items.reflection: Think of a job at work, school or home that only one person really knows how to do. What would happen if they were away for a month?

items.prompt: Which situation is a real bus factor risk rather than just a busy person?
choices: Only Tomas knows why a workaround exists, so others avoid the script
Maya has many tickets, but two teammates could take any of them at once
A teammate reviews slowly, but reviews are shared across four people
The team has no style guide, though all code reads consistently anyway
items.explanation: Only Tomas's case has knowledge that nobody else can supply. The others are workload or process issues with cover available.

choices: Team B is stronger, because clear single ownership removes confusion
Team B is fragile despite equal headcount: any absence stalls a job
Team A wastes time, because duplicated knowledge sits unused
They are equal, because both teams have exactly five people
items.explanation: Bus factor is about coverage per job, not headcount. Team B has a bus factor of one on every job.

items.prompt: Priya gives 14 days' notice. What did the notice change?
choices: How concentrated the knowledge is
How much time the team has to react
How many people can run the job without help
items.explanation: Notice buys reaction time. The concentration was already there.

items.prompt: How do a resignation and a sudden absence compare?
choices: Only the sudden absence is a real risk
Only the resignation is a real risk
They expose the same underlying risk
items.explanation: Both expose one person holding the knowledge.

items.prompt: Where did the risk live before Priya resigned?
choices: In Priya's decision to resign from the company
In the length of her notice period
In only one person being able to run the job
items.explanation: The concentration existed for three years before notice.

items.prompt: Why was the three-sentence runbook a warning sign?
choices: It was far too long for anyone on the team to read
Only Priya ever needed it, so nobody else had learned the job
It had been written by the wrong person for the job
items.explanation: A thin runbook often means one person carried the knowledge in their head.

items.prompt: If notice is the only protection a team has, what is true?
choices: Its resilience depends on being lucky
It is fully protected against every absence
It has no risk to worry about
items.explanation: Sudden absences arrive without warning, so protection that depends on notice is fragile.

items.prompt: Which absence gives the team zero days to react?
choices: Two weeks' notice
A planned month of leave
A sudden hospital stay
items.explanation: Only an unplanned absence arrives with no warning.

items.prompt: Is two weeks always enough to hand over three years of knowledge?
choices: Yes: two weeks is always sufficient
No: some of it will only reach partial coverage
Yes: provided the person works much longer hours
items.explanation: Time-limited handoffs rarely carry everything across at full independence.

items.prompt: When is the best time to find a bus factor problem?
choices: On the person's last day
Before anyone has left
After the first incident
items.explanation: Early, the expert is available and the team can learn without a deadline.

items.prompt: Marcus's first thought is 'two weeks is enough for a proper handoff.' What does that thought miss?
choices: Two weeks is too long, so Priya will lose all motivation to teach the team
A handoff is the departing person's job and not the manager's
Notice periods only matter in companies with formal contracts
Notice buys reaction time but leaves the concentration in place
items.explanation: The risk was a single head holding the knowledge, and that was true long before notice.
items.reference:
Notice changes time, not risk
📅 With notice: 14 days to react
🚑 Without notice: 0 days to react
Same cause either way: one person can run the job
Why: the risk lives in the concentration, which exists before anyone resigns; notice only decides how long you have to react.
items.learnMore:
Time to react vs. size of the risk

A notice period is a bonus that arrives with some departures. It buys time to respond to a risk that was already there, which is why the best time to act is before anyone leaves.

Common mistake

Treating the arrival of notice as the moment the risk appeared.
items.reflection: Where in your own work would a sudden absence be a surprise, and what would you want written down or shared today?

items.prompt: Team X finds its single expert only when she resigns with 30 days' notice. Team Y finds the same kind of gap in a quarterly review while the expert is happy. What did Team Y gain?
choices: Time to fix the concentration on its own terms, with no deadline
A lower chance that the expert will ever leave the team at all
A longer notice period than the one Team X was given
A guarantee that no documentation or pairing will ever be needed again on this team
items.explanation: Finding it early changes when the work is done, not who leaves. Calm teaching beats a countdown.

choices: How many pairing sessions the team has time to run before the last day
Which responsibilities are most dangerous to leave without cover
Whether Priya is able to explain a live failure aloud to the successor
What the runbook can still be expanded to include before she leaves
items.explanation: Priorities come from the map and the stakes, not from the notice. Everything that needs Priya's time is what disappears.

items.prompt: What is a knowledge map?
choices: A network diagram of all the servers the team runs
A ranked list of everyone's favourite tools and habits
A grid of responsibilities against people, scored by independence
items.explanation: It makes who can do what visible in one place.

items.prompt: On the map, what does a 0 mean?
choices: Fully independent
No exposure at all
Has seen it but cannot run it
items.explanation: A 0 is no exposure; a 3 is full independence.

items.prompt: On the map, what does a 3 mean?
choices: Has seen it once
No exposure at all
Fully independent
items.explanation: A 3 means the person can run it without support.

items.prompt: What does a score of 1 mean?
choices: Has seen it but could not run it unsupervised
Could run it with some support
Fully independent and also able to teach it to others
items.explanation: A 1 is exposure, not ability.

items.prompt: A row has one 3 and every other score is 0 or 1. What is its bus factor?
choices: Two
One
Four
items.explanation: Only one person is independent, so a single absence stalls it.

items.prompt: Why not just ask each person whether they could cover?
choices: People never answer such questions
Self-assessment often overstates real ability
Managers are never allowed to discuss who covers what
items.explanation: Watching feels like knowing; the map separates the two.

items.prompt: Does the map predict who will leave?
choices: Yes: it ranks who is most likely to quit next
No: it only makes existing concentration visible
Yes: it lists the people who are planning to resign
items.explanation: It describes coverage, not intent.

items.prompt: How often should the map be reviewed?
choices: Once, when the team is formed
Only at the moment when somebody hands in notice
Regularly, as systems and people change
items.explanation: A one-off map goes stale as soon as the team or systems change.

items.prompt: Scores for Dev, Eli and Fay. Release signing: 3, 1, 0. Alert tuning: 3, 3, 0. Vendor invoices: 2, 2, 3. On-call: 3, 2, 2. Which row matches the rule 'one 3, everyone else 0 or 1'?
choices: Alert tuning: 3, 3, 0
Vendor invoices: 2, 2, 3
Release signing: 3, 1, 0
On-call: 3, 2, 2
items.explanation: Alert tuning has two 3s. Vendor invoices has one 3 but others at 2. On-call has others who can run it with support.
items.reference:
The knowledge map scale
0  no exposure
1  has seen it, could not run it alone
2  could run it with some support
3  fully independent
Why: scores are about what a person can actually do, so a row with only one 3 is a bus factor of one.
items.learnMore:
Mapping instead of sensing

A grid of responsibilities against people, scored by independence, turns a vague worry about one expert into a list of specific, comparable gaps. Writing both scores next to each other is what exposes the difference between watching and doing.

Common mistake

Scoring someone a 2 or 3 because they were in the room once.
items.reflection: Pick one responsibility you hold. Who could really run it without you today, and how would you know?

items.prompt: Dan says 'I kind of know billing reconciliation, I have watched Priya work on it.' What score fits, and why is writing it down useful?
choices: A 2: months of watching count as running it with some support
A 3: long familiarity is the same thing as full independence
A 0: anything short of actually running it counts as no exposure
A 1: he has seen it but could not run it, a gap the map exposes
items.explanation: Watching is exposure, a 1. The map matters because it puts that next to Priya's 3 instead of leaving two vague impressions.

items.prompt: A manager scores a teammate 2 on a payments job because 'she was in the room during the last incident.' What is wrong?
choices: Being present is not the same as running it with real accountability
The map should only ever be filled in by the teammates themselves
Incidents are too rare to be a fair basis for any score at all
Payments jobs should never appear on a knowledge map in the first place
items.explanation: Scores must be earned by doing. Inflated scores hide the exact risk the map exists to surface.

items.prompt: Which practice writes the stable 'what and how' down for self-serve use?
choices: Documentation
Rotation
Pairing or shadowing
items.explanation: Documentation captures what can be explained in advance.

items.prompt: Which practice transfers judgment calls while real work happens?
choices: Documentation
Pairing or shadowing
A quarterly report to leadership
items.explanation: Judgment surfaces during live work, so it is best learned alongside it.

items.prompt: Which practice makes a second person actually own the work for a stretch?
choices: Documentation alone
Pairing alone
Rotation of ownership
items.explanation: Owning the work is what proves the reasoning holds up.

items.prompt: Which practice is a standing rule that two people always own a responsibility?
choices: Documentation alone
One-off shadowing
Deliberate redundancy
items.explanation: Redundancy is a permanent norm, not a one-time fix.

items.prompt: Can documentation alone transfer judgment nobody made explicit?
choices: No: it only holds what was written
Yes: a long enough runbook covers everything
Yes: if it is shared
items.explanation: Unwritten judgment cannot be copied from a page that never held it.

items.prompt: What does pairing need that documentation does not?
choices: A separate approval from the finance team
A new tool installed on every laptop
Both people's time at the same moment
items.explanation: Pairing is live, so both people must be present.

items.prompt: Why does rotation test more than pairing?
choices: The expert gets to take extra time off
The second person has to produce the reasoning
It needs far less preparation than a runbook
items.explanation: Pairing shows the learner can follow; rotation shows they can lead.

items.prompt: Is there one best practice for raising bus factor?
choices: Yes: documentation always suffices
No: each closes a different gap
Yes: rotation always suffices
items.explanation: The four complement each other.

items.prompt: A thorough runbook exists, and only Priya has ever run the job. What does the best other person's score look like after reading it?
choices: A 3, since every step is now written down in full detail for them
About a 1: the steps are known on paper but have not been run
A 2, since reading the steps counts as running them with support
Still a 0, since reading a runbook never changes anyone's score
items.explanation: A reader has seen the steps, which is a 1. Running them is what raises it.
items.reference:
Four practices, four gaps
📄 Documentation: the stable steps
🤝 Pairing: the judgment behind them
🔁 Rotation: real ownership, tested
🛡️ Redundancy: a standing two-owner rule
Why: each practice closes a different gap, so documentation alone leaves a reader at about a 1.
items.learnMore:
Why one practice is not enough

Writing things down transfers what can be written. Judgment shows up only when something breaks, which is why pairing and then ownership are needed to move a score from 1 to a tested 3.

Common mistake

Writing a thorough runbook and declaring the bus factor fixed.
items.reflection: For something you know well, what part could you write down, and what part could you only teach by doing it next to someone?

items.prompt: Wren shadowed a live failure and watched Priya retry twice, then escalate. Which practice did that, and what did it transfer?
choices: Pairing: the judgment behind a call the runbook did not yet hold
Documentation: stable steps that anyone can follow at a later date
Rotation: ownership of the job for a full stretch of weeks
Redundancy: a standing rule that two people always own the job
items.explanation: Shadowing a real failure is pairing, and the judgment call was exactly what documentation lacked.

choices: Rotation spreads on-call duty around so that people feel far less tired
Rotation produces documentation as a side effect, which counts as a 3

Rotation replaces the need for any earlier pairing or notes
items.explanation: A 3 means independent, and independence is only shown when the expert is not the backstop.

items.prompt: What does deliberate redundancy cost?
choices: Ongoing time from two people on one job
A one-off fee that is paid once at the start
Nothing, it is free insurance
items.explanation: Every week of redundancy is time not spent on other work.

items.prompt: Should every responsibility be staffed two-deep?
choices: Yes: every row without exception
Yes: except the most important ones
No: bound it to high-stakes rows
items.explanation: Redundancy everywhere costs more than the risk it removes.

items.prompt: Which responsibility most deserves redundancy?
choices: A rarely used report script
The office plant watering rota
Payment deploy approval
items.explanation: Money is at stake, so a single point of failure is costly.

items.prompt: Which responsibility probably needs only documentation?
choices: Security-critical access decisions for the whole team
A rarely used internal reporting script
Payment deploy approval, which touches customer money
items.explanation: A slow fix costs little there, so a runbook is enough.

items.prompt: What risk does uniform redundancy trade for?
choices: More unexpected resignations among the team
Faster hiring of brand new people for the job
Not enough new work getting built
items.explanation: Spending capacity on duplication leaves less for everything else.

items.prompt: Are security-critical access decisions worth redundancy?
choices: No: they are never important enough
No: documentation always replaces it
Yes: stalled access is costly
items.explanation: A bus factor of one there could block the whole team.

items.prompt: For onboarding new hires, how much redundancy is enough?
choices: Partial: a second trained person
Full permanent two-deep staffing
None, because it is optional
items.explanation: Some cover helps, but full redundancy costs more than the risk.

items.prompt: What decides how much redundancy a row gets?
choices: How long the job has existed in the company
How severe a bus factor of one would be
How many people like the job
items.explanation: Stakes of failure, not age or taste, set the level.

items.prompt: Limited second-person training can go to one of three: signing customer-facing app releases, formatting a monthly internal chart, or rotating the retro facilitator. Which first?
choices: The monthly chart: it recurs on a fixed schedule every single month
The retro facilitator: it affects every team member in the room
All three equally, so that no row is ever left without cover
Signing releases: a single absence blocks what customers receive
items.explanation: Pick by the damage of a bus factor of one. Releases block customers; the others are cheap to cover or skip.
items.reference:
Assumed model: chance nobody can run the job
0 trained: 100%
1 trained: 33%
2 trained: 11%
3 trained: 4%, 4 trained: 1%
Why: teaching numbers only, but the shape shows the first extra person removes most of the risk, so redundancy belongs where stakes are high.
items.learnMore:
Spend redundancy where it pays

Every extra trained person costs time, and the benefit shrinks with each addition. A team picks rows by the damage a bus factor of one would cause, and covers the rest with documentation and some pairing.

Common mistake

Applying two-deep staffing to everything and calling the team safe.
items.reflection: Which responsibility in your life would be most costly to leave with one person, and which could simply be written down?

items.prompt: A director says 'make everything two-deep and we never worry again.' What is the strongest reply?
choices: Agree: resilience is always worth more than all of the capacity that it uses up
That cuts capacity for new work and only moves risk; choose rows by stakes
Disagree: documentation alone covers every row without exception
Agree, but only for the jobs the director personally relies on
items.explanation: Duplication has a weekly cost, so it must be spent where failure hurts most.

items.explanation: Partial means some cover is worth paying for, but the stakes do not justify a permanent two-deep rule.

items.prompt: Marcus has 14 days. Where does he start?
choices: With the longest runbook that he is able to write
With a map scoped to what Priya touches
With a team meeting about the morale of everyone
items.explanation: He needs to know which rows are at risk before choosing what to do.

items.prompt: Why not lift everything to a 3 within two weeks?
choices: Everything on the team is already covered well
A score of three is forbidden by the company
There is not enough time for that
items.explanation: A deadline forces a choice about what reaches a 2.

items.prompt: Which row needs a real 2 by day 14?
choices: The billing reconciliation job
The quarterly reconciliation report
The vendor relationship
items.explanation: Nobody except Priya can fix it, and it runs nightly.

items.prompt: Why does the vendor relationship get only a document handoff?
choices: It is the least important thing Priya does
Priya refuses to discuss it
Dan is already a 2 on that row
items.explanation: Someone can already run it with support, so it needs notes, not scarce live time.

items.prompt: Why does the quarterly report need no action?
choices: The team never needs it
Priya will do it from home
Sam already owns it completely
items.explanation: Sam scores 3, so the row is already covered.

items.prompt: What does 'triage' mean here?
choices: Deciding what gets scarce time first
Writing every runbook at once
Sharing the news with the whole company
items.explanation: Triage orders work by urgency and gap.

items.prompt: Which two rows get the live pairing time?
choices: Vendor relationship and quarterly report
Billing job and payment deploy approval
Quarterly report and the billing job
items.explanation: These two have the lowest cover and the sharpest consequences.

items.prompt: Why confirm where redundancy already exists?
choices: To reduce the final salary that Priya will be paid
To avoid spending hours where it is not needed
To remove the need for making any plan at all
items.explanation: Scarce hours should go to real gaps.

items.prompt: Priya also holds a password-rotation duty. Scores: Dan 2, Wren 2, Sam 0. Live pairing is already spent on the billing job and payment approval. What does Marcus do with this row?
choices: Make it the third pairing priority since Sam scores a zero on it
Ignore it, because any task with a score of 2 is safe forever
Hand it to Dan with a short note, as two people can already run it
Delay the billing job pairing so this row is handled first
items.explanation: Two people at a 2 means cover exists. A document handoff is proportionate.
items.reference:
Day-1 triage (Dan / Wren / Sam)
🧾 Billing job: 0 / 1 / 0, first priority
